title: Internet suspended in Uganda, 13 January 2021
overview: In January 2021, authorities ordered a total shutdown of the Internet in Uganda during the general elections. After announcing that access to social media platforms would be restricted, a full shutdown was implemented at 7pm on the evening before election day, cutting access for over 45 million citizens.
data_analysis:
OONI

In the days leading up to the election, access to Google Play Store, major social media platforms and circumvention tools was blocked (even when the OTT (Over the Top) tax, commonly referred to as the “Social Media Tax”, was paid.

The following chart aggregates OONI measurement coverage from Uganda in January 2021, illustrating the blocking of the Google Play Store (play.google.com) and many social media websites (such as Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram).

Chart: Blocking of Google Play Store and social media websites in Uganda in January 2021 (source: OONI MAT).

From the above chart, we can see that the testing of Google Play Store and social media websites (excluding youtube.com) started to present anomalies in the days leading up to the election, while we observe a complete absence of OONI measurements during the days of the reported Internet outage (between the evening of 13th January to the morning of 18th January 2021). 

Even though Internet connectivity in Uganda was restored on 18th January 2021, access to social media remained blocked. Notably, Ugandan ISPs only appear to have started blocking access to YouTube on 18th January 2021 (as illustrated in the above chart), even though the platform was not included on the OTT list of taxed platforms.

In addition to the blocking of social media websites, OONI data shows the blocking of instant messaging apps as well. Starting from 12th January 2021, OONI data collected from Uganda on the testing of WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Telegram apps presented signs of blocking on several networks, as illustrated through the chart below.

The above chart aggregates OONI measurement coverage from the testing of the WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, and Telegram apps on several networks in Uganda in January 2021. We can see that several ISPs started blocking the apps leading up to the election, and resumed the block after the internet outage (from 18th January 2021 onwards). This pattern is consistent with what is observed for the blocking of social media websites, discussed previously. During this period, OONI data shows that access to certain circumvention tool websites (such as protonvpn.com) appears to have been blocked as well, though both Tor and Psiphon appear to have worked throughout the election period.Learn more through OONI’s research report.

Oracle Internet Intelligence and IODA

As of 13 January 2021, data available from Oracle's Internet Intelligence and IODA show a drop in the visibility of IP prefixes through BGP in Uganda by 15-25% between 13:30 and 16:00UTC, followed by larger drop reaching to 75% by 20:00UTC until 18 January 2021 8:00UTC when traffic started to get back to normal indicating end of the shutdown. The previous directive on blocking social media services is still effective.

Data from Uganda Internet Exchange Point showing huge drop in traffic, from an average of 5Gbits to a mere average of 280Mbits

Google Transparency Report
local_impact:
The country experienced a widespread Internet blackout that lasted four days, starting on 13 January and ending in the morning of 18 January 2021. Domestic Internet traffic in the country fell by 95 percent as a result of the government’s orders. And, as Ugandans headed to the polls, they were unable to access information, communicate with loved ones, or simply go about their daily business.

The shutdown follows months of disruption to the flow of information and crackdowns on the media. CPJ reported that Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni had announced that the government was enforcing a social media shutdown after Facebook closed several government-linked accounts for allegedly being part of an effort to manipulate the election debate.

This is not the first time Uganda had restricted access during elections: MTN Uganda reported a similar order in 2016, when access to social media was cut during the elections and the presidential inauguration. Internet shutdowns during elections impact the ability of citizens to get accurate information from trusted sources when they need it the most and can hinder their ability to exercise their civic duties.

title: Internet suspended in Iran, 13 June 2025
overview: From the morning of Friday, 13 June, Internet in Iran suffered disruptions with the Iranian Ministry of Communications announcement that these restrictions are temporary. The measurements show further drop between 14:00 and 20:00 on 17 June, followed by a near total shutdown as of 12:50 UTC on 18 June. There was an increase in traffic as of 03:00 UTC on 21 June indicating a partial restoration of service. Full service appeared to be restored as of 05:00 UTC on 25 June.
data_analysis: Measurements on Cloudflare Radar indicate drop in traffic from 13 June with further drop on 17 June then a near full shutdown as of midday of 18 June, and then a partial increase as of early morning of 21 June. Full service appears to have resumed from 05:00 UTC on 25 June.
local_impact: The Iranian government is reported to have significantly restricted access to the Internet within the country from 13 June, and is reported to be planning to fully shut down the Internet and and replace it with “an intranet service“ overnight on the 17th. The significant loss of connectivity comes after several days of military conflict between Israel and Iran, with unnamed government officials citing the need to disrupt covert Israeli operations as the reason to shutdown Internet access.
cause_documentation:
Announcement by the Iranian Ministry of Communication on 13 June stating that "in view of the special conditions of the country and with the measures of the competent authorities, temporary restrictions have been imposed on the country's internet." This announcement was reported on the official news agency, Tasnim, and Mehr News. Local News agencies also reported that further restrictions were implemented on 18 June to "prevent enemy abuse"

The New York Times also reported that Iranian government is reported to have significantly restricted access to the Internet within the country, and is reported to be planning to fully shut down the Internet and and replace it with “an intranet service“ overnight on the 17th. title: Internet suspended in Bocas del Toro, Panama, 14 June 2025
overview: On 14 June 2025, Bocas del Toro, Panama, experienced an unexpected disruption in internet connectivity that lasted for 47 hours. This interruption preceded the declaration of a state of emergency in the province on 20 June 2025, amid ongoing protests against reforms to the Social Security Fund (CSS), pensions, and retirements. Following the state of emergency declaration, Panama's telecom regulator, the National Public Services Authority (ASEP), issued an official order to telecommunication and internet service providers. This order mandated the suspension of cellular mobile telephony and internet services for residential users in Bocas del Toro, while excluding essential sectors such as health, commerce, and government services.
data_analysis: IODA recorded drops in Internet traffic on 14 June 2025 to 30 June 2025.
local_impact: On 21 June 2025, ASEP issued a follow-up statement specifying that the internet shutdown in Bocas del Toro applied exclusively to residential users, with exemptions for critical sectors such as health, commerce, and government services. This selective suspension was part of the government's response to ongoing protests against reforms to the Social Security Fund (CSS), pensions, and retirements, which had intensified in the region. While the measure was initially scheduled to conclude on 25 June 2025, the government extended the restrictions until Sunday, 29 June, directly impacting all residential internet users in the province. The prolonged disruption raised concerns about access to essential online services and the broader implications for human rights in the digital age, particularly in a province where internet connectivity is vital for daily life and economic activities.

title: Internet suspended in Balochistan, Pakistan, 5 August 2025
overview: The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has reportedly ordered Internet Service Providers to suspend mobile Internet services in the Balochistan region due to security concerns.
data_analysis: It’s difficult to measure the effect of local/regional Internet shutdowns, as most measurements are done at a country level. Learn more
local_impact:
The Balochistan Post reported that the suspension was enforced due to possible security threats amid heightened tensions around Pakistan’s National Day celebrations.

A government spokesperson told international news agency Reuters that armed groups had been using the Internet to coordinate activities. The suspension, he said, was intended to disrupt such communications.

A reported notification issued by the PTA confirmed that mobile internet services will remain suspended across Balochistan until 31 August.

According to one report, a Senator and senior lawyer have submitted a motion in the Senate for debate on the Internet shutdown, terming it a matter of urgent public importance.

Balochistan is one of Pakistan's largest provinces by size, bordering Afghanistan and Iran. More than half (8.5 M) of its 15 million inhabitants are cell phone subscribers.

title: Internet suspended in Kurdistan, Iraq, 23 August 2025
overview: The Kurdistan Regional Government in Iraq ordered Internet services to be suspended on the morning of 23 August 2025 between 6:30 and 7:45 local time (+3 UTC). This regional shutdown is part of a series of shutdowns during the public school exams, which are expected to happen every Saturday, Monday, and Wednesday until 8 September.
data_analysis: Cloudflare Radar data shows drops in Cloudflare traffic in key networks operating mainly in Kurdistan region in Iraq, namely Kurdistan NET (KNET).

The affected networks include KNET — Kurdistan Net (AS206206), Newroz Telecom (AS21277), IQ Online (AS48492), and KorekTel (AS59625). These networks combined have around 20% of the overall Iraqi market but serve the vast majority of the population in the Kurdistan region.

title: Content blocking in Nepal, 3 September 2025
overview: The Nepal Ministry for Communication and Information Technology (MoCIT) ordered the Nepal Telecommunication Authority (NTA) to make unregistered social media sites inactive until they are registered in Nepal under the Social Media Directives 2080.
data_analysis:
OONI's Web Connectivity Test shows anomalies connecting to the most popular banned social media services.

Note that tests for Telegram have been showing similar results since mid-July.

Google Transparency Report also shows a drop in traffic to YouTube from 6 to 9 September.
local_impact:
The directive follows the MoCIT's setting a seven-day deadline for 26 foreign and domestic platforms to register, which expired at midnight on Thursday, 4 September. The platforms included: Facebook, Facebook Messenger, Instagram, YouTube, WhatsApp, Twitter (X), LinkedIn, Snapchat, Reddit, Discord, Pinterest, Signal, Threads, WeChat, Quora, Tumblr, Clubhouse, Mastodon, Rumble, MeWe, VK, Line, IMO, Zalo, Soul, and Hamro Patro.

The government had previously ordered the NTA to instruct local Internet service providers to block Telegram (18 July 2025).

According to reports, of the 26 social media platforms that were issued the orders, TikTok, Viber, Nimbuzz, WeTalk, and Poppo Live were the only ones to complete the registration, and Telegram and GlobalLink were still in the registration process.

Protests Lead to Government Suspending Ban

Protestors took to the streets of Kathmandu on Monday, 8 September, to voice their opposition to the bans and anger towards the government over “corruption and a weak economy.” The resulting unrest and letters of petition from the community led the Ministry to backtrack on its orders on Tuesday, 9 September.
cause_documentation:
The Ministry of Communication and Information Technology under the Government of Nepal introduced Directives for Managing the Use of Social Media, 2080 (2023) (“Social Media Directives”) through publication in the Nepal Gazette dated 27 November 2023. The Social Media Directives establish a regulatory framework for the operation, oversight, and compliance of social media platforms within Nepal.

﻿Any individual, company, or organization intending to operate a social media platform must enlist with the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology (“Ministry”). If the social media platform fails to enlist, the Ministry can prohibit such platforms from operating within Nepal. Learn more.

﻿After nearly two years of asking social media platorfms to register, the Ministry ordered the Nepal Telecommunication Authority to issue the following directive on 28 August 2025 to register before midnight 4 September 2025 or else be banned from being accessed in the country.

🚨BIG: Nepal Telecommunications Authority has issued a directive requiring nearly all major social media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, X (Twitter), LinkedIn, Snapchat, Reddit, Discord and more to register locally in #Nepal. pic.twitter.com/o0t6btJMwu

— VAISHNAV 🇮🇳 (@VaishnavSharan7) September 5, 2025
experiences:
What’s happening in Nepal mirrors “this broader pattern of controlling the narrative and controlling of stories emerging from the ground,” said Aditya Vashistha, an assistant professor of information science at Cornell University. “This has happened several times in the neighboring countries India, Pakistan, Bangladesh. So this is nothing new — in fact, I would say this is taken from the playbook, which is now very established, of trying to control social media narratives.”

“Governments absolutely have a valid interest in seeking to regulate social media platforms. This is such a daily part of our lives and in our business. And it is certainly reasonable for authorities to sit down and say we want to develop rules for the road,” said Kian Vesteinsson, senior research analyst for technology and democracy at the Washington-based nonprofit Freedom House.

“But what we see in Nepal is that wholesale blocks as a means of enforcing a set of rules for social media companies results in wildly disproportionate harms. These measures that were put in place in Nepal (cut) tens of millions of people off from platforms that they used to express themselves, to conduct daily business, to speak with their families, to go to school, to get healthcare information.” — Associated Press

title: Internet suspended in Ethiopia, 11 June 2019
overview: Ethiopia experienced a complete internet blackout on June 11, 2019, lasting approximately 5 hours from 7:00 UTC to 12:00 UTC. The country's sole commercial internet provider, Ethio Telecom, cut connectivity nationwide, reportedly to prevent cheating during national high school examinations. This was the first of three related shutdowns that would occur over a 3-day period (June 11-14). Following the series of complete blackouts, selective blocking of messaging platforms WhatsApp and Telegram occurred from June 15-18, and SMS services within the country were also disrupted during this same week.
data_analysis:
The country's sole internet provider, Ethio Telecom, discontinued its services in three separate blackouts between June 11-14. 

  - Shutdown 1: June 11, from 7:00 UTC to 12:00 UTC (5 hours)
  - Shutdown 2: June 11-12, from 17:00 UTC to 6:30 UTC (13.5 hours)
  - Shutdown 3: June 12-14, from 17:45 UTC to 12:15 UTC (42.5 hours)

Ethio Telecom issued an [apology](https://web.archive.org/web/20190619122350/https:/twitter.com/ethiotelecom_/status/1141013304762146817) on June 18 without providing details of the cause of the interruption, however press reports allege that the blackout was a measure to prevent secondary students cheating during the annual national examinations.

local_impact: [Local businesses](https://web.archive.org/web/20240612032041/https://edition.cnn.com/2019/06/17/africa/ethiopia-internet-outage-intl/index.html) that rely on connectivity, such as tour operators, were either forced to close, or use VPN to connect to the Internet and access messaging platforms. Some resorted to using business centers at luxury hotels, which appear to still have Internet access. Popular taxi service ZayRide was also affected, leaving its drivers with no work for a week. [Press reports](https://web.archive.org/web/20190724155310/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-06-13/exam-cheats-cited-in-three-day-internet-shutdown-in-ethiopia), and a source speaking to TechCrunch on background, said Ethiopia’s internet stoppage was done to stop students from cheating on national exams, which took place this week.

title: Content blocking in Venezuela, 24 May 2019
overview: The state-owned Internet service provider CANTV (AS8048) implemented a block on YouTube and Periscope on May 24 during the Venezuelan presidential crisis of 2019.
data_analysis:
OONI data and other measurements by [VEsinFiltro](https://x.com/vesinfiltro/status/1131953266567319552) show the blocking of YouTube and Periscope on CANTV (AS8048) the state-owned ISP that is also the most important service provider.

![OONI measurements for AS8048 (CANTV)](/2025_pulse_check/14825/OONI-AS8048-2019-05-24.png)

[VEsinFiltro reports](https://x.com/vesinfiltro/status/1131972015555043328) that Periscope was blocked using SNI filtering, while YouTube was blocked using IP blocking, affecting Google Drive, Calendar and many other google services
local_impact:
During the closing event of the Plan País International Congress, held at the Andrés Bello Catholic University (UCAB) in Caracas, YouTube and Periscope were blocked by CANTV (ASN: AS8048), the main internet provider and a state-owned company in Venezuela.

This block occurred in the context of the 2019 Venezuelan presidential crisis, which pits Nicolás Maduro against Juan Guaidó, and this pattern of blocks since January 2019 is part of a "strong escalation in internet censorship and control" according to Conexion Segura y Libre's VEsinFiltro program. The short and precisely timed blocks, such as this one, are frequently used to silence the live broadcasts of statements and public acts by Juan Guaidó.

The block also affected multiple Google services, including Google Drive, Google Calendar, Google Meet, and Google Chat.

title: Content blocking in Venezuela, 28 September 2024
overview: Venezuelan ISPs have blocked access to X (formerly Twitter), Signal and TikTok as part of a broader pattern of digital censorship. X and Signal have been blocked in Venezuela since 8 August 2024, amidst protests against disputed election results announced by authorities. On 28 September 2024, TikTok was also blocked for approximately 7 hours. These measures align with Venezuela's history of digital censorship, where social media platforms are frequently restricted during politically sensitive periods.
data_analysis:
On 28 September 2024, TikTok was blocked for 7 hours on at least 7 different ISPs as reported by VE sin Filtro, based on ad-hoc and OONI Measurements.

Concurrently, on 8 August 2024, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro ordered blocking X (formerly Twitter) in Venezuela for an initial period of 10 days that was extended without clarification, as reported by VE sin Filtro monitoring project of the local digital rights organization Conexión Segura y Libre (CSL). Later that day, the domain signal.org was also blocked, affecting the messaging application's operation.

Different ISPs implemented the block in different ways, but some of the affected domains are:

  • x.com
  • api.x.com
  • api.twitter.com
  • abs.twimg.com
  • pbs.twimg.com
local_impact: The simultaneous blocking of TikTok, Signal and X (formerly Twitter) in september 2024 created a significant information vacuum in Venezuela, disrupting essential communication channels for citizens, journalists, and civil society organizations. This severely impaired the public’s ability to access real-time news, document events, and coordinate civic activities during a period of acute political sensitivity. The disruption was observed across multiple Internet Service Providers (ISPs), including the state-owned CANTV and major private operators, highlighting the centralized nature of digital censorship in the country. This multi-platform blockade underscores the heightened vulnerability of digital rights in Venezuela and demonstrates the strategic use of network interference to suppress the free flow of information during critical political transitions.
cause_documentation: On 8 August 2024, Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro ordered the suspension of X (Twitter) for an initial period of 10 days, citing the need to "preserve peace and social stability.". However, the block has continued indefinitely beyond the announced deadline. Meanwhile, TikTok was inaccessible for 7 hours on September 28, 2024 without any public or official order.

title: Content blocking in Venezuela, 4 January 2025
overview:
In January 2025, Venezuela significantly intensified digital censorship block websites of internet circumvention tools and public DNS servers, severely limiting citizens' access to uncensored information. Beginning as early as January 4 and intensifying around January 6, state-owned ISP CANTV and private operators. Key targets included:

 

  • Public DNS Servers: Over 30 public DNS services were restricted between January 4 and January 11, including major resolvers like Google Public DNS (8.8.8.8) and Cloudflare (1.1.1.1), which are crucial for bypassing content blocks.
  • VPNs and Tor: Major ISPs blocked at least 21 prominent VPN websites and the website Tor network, starting around January 6 and intensifying on January 9.
